source.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy

record.tranche_reason: The paper takes neuron polysemanticity and superposition as motivation for SAE feature decomposition, but its own measurements concern SAE features, not neurons in the underlying language models. It neither tests the listed neuron claims nor reports neuron-level outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper asserts that neurons in LLMs mix concepts as background motivation, but those assertions and cited results are not new results and are not rows. Its original empirical results measure SAE feature interpretability and decoder redundancy. Because SAE features are not neurons, those findings are recorded as related but not covered by any listed claim version. The paper also reports broader SAE metrics for reconstruction, sparsity, and dead features; those are not included here because they do not directly measure the claim’s polysemanticity subject.
record.test_reason: The paper takes neuron polysemanticity from superposition as background motivation (Sec. 1, 2.1, citing Elhage et al. 2022). Its own results all concern SAE features: DAME interpretability by dominance quartile, decoder-cosine redundancy, and synthetic SAE concept alignment. It reports no measurement of polysemanticity in neurons of image classifiers or language-model MLPs. It does not test superposition or other causes at the neuron level. It does not compare neuron polysemanticity across base-model architectures. The one neuron-level figure (Bills et al.: about 0.33% of GPT-2 XL neurons score ≥0.8) is cited, not new. None of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the most dominant SAE features are systematically less monosemantic and more redundant under their DAME and decoder-cosine measures. They argue that standard evaluations miss this, and they recommend dominance-stratified checks before SAE features are used for attribution or intervention.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce the cited neuron-level methods. It evaluates SAE features using dominance-stratified DAME ranking and decoder-direction cosine similarity, rather than examining or scoring individual neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: For SAE-feature DAME scores, the measured Q1 gap varies by SAE family and architecture; the paper also varies explanation budget and explainer/judge pairing, and reports that the Q1 deficit persists across those tested checks. Redundancy analysis depends on decoder cosine thresholds and dead-feature filtering; the authors report threshold robustness and explain that filtering changes the apparent quartile distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: On two pre-selected SAEs, DAME shows Q1 deficits of −11.83 and −9.50 pp. A feature-uniform binary AutoInterp assay on the same features shows +0.13 and +0.35 pp. Whether dominant SAE features look polysemantic therefore depends on the scoring rule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether SAE features appear polysemantic depends on the scoring rule (activation-ranking vs binary detection) and on dominance-stratified aggregation.

fits_no_version.finding: Highest-dominance SAE features score lower on DAME perfect-ranking accuracy than Q2–Q4 (61.8% vs 64.1%; p=6.76e-8). The gap varies by architecture and family and reverses for GPT2-Small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In evaluated SAEs, dominant features are less interpretable under dominance-aware held-out activation ranking, with variation across architectures and families.

fits_no_version.finding: Decoder-direction redundancy concentrates among high-dominance SAE features (median Q1 endpoint enrichment 1.64×).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-dominance SAE features more often share decoder directions with other features.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic SAEs with known concepts, Q1 features show lower concept alignment and lower held-out support containment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dominant features in synthetic SAEs align less with single ground-truth concepts.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
record.problems: The empirical outcomes concern SAE features, not neurons, so they do not directly establish any of the listed neuron claims. The authors identify LLM-based monosemanticity scoring as a proxy with judge and prompting limitations; they also note limited model, layer, and SAE-family coverage for larger-model checks, hyperparameter-transfer issues, and that some architecture-specific Q1 results are nonsignificant. Ground-truth concept tests are synthetic rather than exhaustive evaluations of real LLM concepts.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable to the neuron-level claim versions: the paper’s additional tables and appendices report further SAE reconstruction, sparsity, dead-feature, redundancy-threshold, and feature-family breakdowns. These are not separate neuron-level outcomes and are not treated as claim-version rows.

untested.parts: No measurement of neurons in image classifiers. The vision discussion (Sec. 2.1) concerns pixel patches as units and is conceptual only.
No count or share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models, and no layer comparison. Neuron mixing is asserted via cited superposition work.
Superposition is invoked as motivation. No test of whether neuron polysemanticity stems from capacity pressure.
No test of neuron polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
Architecture comparisons are across SAE architectures, not base-model activation functions or neuron polysemanticity. No performance trade-off is measured for base networks.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
The paper shows measurement-dependence of SAE-feature interpretability scores, not of neuron polysemanticity.

missing.what: DAME vs binary AutoInterp on the same features (Q1 gap −11.83/−9.50 pp vs +0.13/+0.35 pp). This is an SAE-feature result only, not neuron-level.
missing.versions: none (related to V7 construct but for SAE features)

missing.what: Larger-model check of Q1 deficit: Qwen3-8B/14B/32B at 41.7%/50.0%/41.7% of SAEs; Gemma-2-9B at 75.0%. SAE features only.

record.verdict_notes: All rows concern SAE features. Their versions ['none'] are correct. The record's relation (assumes) and tranche (T4) are kept: the study uses superposition-driven neuron polysemanticity as the premise for SAEs and reports only SAE-evaluation outcomes. Minor state fixes apply to non-significant and reversed family rows. The 'partial' states on r26–r32 are judged against the paper's own Q1-deficit direction and could be 'observed'. This does not affect any neuron version.

versions.untested_parts: No neuron-level tests in image classifiers or InceptionV1; no measurements of neuron responses to image inputs.
No measurements of MLP neurons in transformer language models responding to tokens or contexts.
The paper invokes superposition as background motivation but does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity pressure or compare against alternative causes.
No neuron-level tests of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise in networks with sufficient capacity.

The paper compares SAE architectures and training configurations, not the share of polysemantic neurons across base-network activation functions or architectures, and does not test a neuron-level performance tradeoff.
The paper does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons or determine whether their mixed inputs share a feature.
The paper compares measurements of SAE-feature interpretability, not whether neuron polysemanticity depends on the activation range or explanation score.
